criteria.descriptor: Correctly describes how BPE learns and applies merges, why rare domain strings fragment (byte/subword fallback, no true OOV/UNK), and accurately states that adding tokens requires resizing embeddings that then start random and must be trained. No false claims (e.g. that subword tokenizers drop the word as UNK, or that word-level preserves pretrained embeddings).

Covers all four asked parts — the fragmentation mechanism, the downstream problems (length/cost/truncation and representation), the flaw in the word-level proposal, and at least two concrete mitigations — rather than only explaining the mechanism.

Justifies why fragmentation matters (ties length to cost and truncation, ties fragmentation to weaker representation) and why each recommended fix is preferable to the word-level alternative, including the transfer-learning/compatibility argument and empirical validation via fertility.
Explanation is well-organized and uses correct vocabulary (BPE merges, subword/byte fallback, OOV/UNK, vocabulary size, embedding resize, token fertility) precisely and unambiguously.

expected_answer_points: Explains that BPE/subword tokenizers build a fixed vocabulary by merging frequent adjacent units from a training corpus, and that rare domain strings (SKUs, URLs, code) lack learned merges so they decompose into many small subword/byte pieces — the mechanism that avoids true OOV rather than emitting UNK
Identifies fragmentation consequences: longer sequences drive higher compute/latency (attention scales roughly quadratically with length) and risk max-length truncation of real content
Notes the representational cost: spreading a meaningful term (the SKU) across many weak subword pieces yields a poorer embedding for exactly the tokens the classifier cares about
Rejects word-level tokenization with reasons: it reintroduces OOV/UNK for unseen SKUs, explodes vocabulary size, and is incompatible with the pretrained model's embeddings (loses transfer learning)
Proposes extending the existing tokenizer with domain tokens (add_tokens) plus resizing embeddings, and notes the new embeddings start random and must be trained during fine-tuning

Proposes normalization/preprocessing (e.g. mapping URLs/SKUs to placeholder tokens or training a domain-specific tokenizer) and measuring token fertility / tokens-per-word to justify the choice empirically
common_pitfalls: Claims the subword tokenizer emits [UNK] or loses the SKU entirely, missing that byte-level BPE decomposes into bytes/subwords and has no true OOV
Accepts or half-accepts the word-level proposal without flagging that it recreates the OOV problem, bloats vocabulary, and breaks compatibility with the pretrained embeddings
Says 'just raise max_length' as the fix, ignoring that longer sequences cost more (roughly quadratic attention) and that the representation problem remains
Recommends adding domain tokens but forgets model.resize_token_embeddings, or assumes the new tokens automatically have meaningful embeddings rather than random ones that must be fine-tuned
Confuses this tokenization/fragmentation issue with stemming/lemmatization or treats it as a text-cleaning bug
Blames the token explosion on temperature, model size, or a preprocessing typo instead of the tokenizer's subword mechanism
reference_answer:
Byte-level BPE builds a fixed vocabulary by starting from bytes and greedily merging the most frequent adjacent pairs in its training corpus (general web text). At inference it re-applies those learned merges. Strings that were rare in that corpus — SKUs, URLs, code — have few or no dedicated merges, so they fall back to many small subword/byte pieces. This is by design: subword tokenizers avoid true out-of-vocabulary tokens by decomposing unknown strings rather than emitting [UNK], and the price is fragmentation (high "fertility", i.e. tokens per word).

Consequences: sequences get much longer, so you pay more compute and latency (self-attention scales quadratically in length) and risk hitting the model's max-length limit and truncating real content; the SKU's meaning is also smeared across many weakly-related pieces, giving a poorer representation of exactly the tokens that matter for this task.

Switching to word-level is a poor fix: it reintroduces the OOV/UNK problem (every unseen SKU becomes UNK), explodes vocabulary size, and — critically — is incompatible with the pretrained embeddings you are trying to leverage, discarding transfer learning.

What I would do: keep the subword tokenizer but add a curated set of frequent domain tokens (tokenizer.add_tokens) and call model.resize_token_embeddings; note the new rows are randomly initialized and must be learned during fine-tuning. Complement this by normalizing high-cardinality noise — replace arbitrary URLs/SKUs with placeholder tokens — and measure token fertility before/after to justify the change against sequence-length and accuracy budgets.
